prompt: Which statement correctly describes the VLAN identifier in an ordinary 802.1Q tag?
options: It is 16 bits, providing VLAN IDs 1 through 65534.
It is 12 bits, with usable VLAN identifiers 1 through 4094.
It is 8 bits, providing VLAN IDs 1 through 254.
It is 32 bits, with one separate identifier for each IP subnet.
explanation: The VID is a 12-bit field. Values 0 and 4095 are reserved, which leaves 1–4094.

whyWrong.0: The 16-bit TPID identifies the tag format, not the VLAN.
whyWrong.2: The VID is 12 bits, not 8.
whyWrong.3: The whole tag is 32 bits, and the VID is only part of it.

prompt: Two switch ports are both set to dynamic auto. What is the DTP result?
options: A trunk because each side advertises willingness to trunk.
An error-disabled link caused by a negotiation conflict.
A nontrunking link because neither side initiates trunk negotiation.
A trunk carrying only the common native VLAN.
explanation: Dynamic auto only responds to a trunk request and never sends one. Two auto ports leave the link as an access link.

whyWrong.0: Auto is passive, so neither side advertises a request to trunk.
whyWrong.1: Auto with auto is a normal access link, not an error-disable trigger.
whyWrong.3: There is no partial trunk that carries only the native VLAN.

prompt: Which two statements describe switchport nonegotiate on a static trunk? (Choose two.)
options: It suppresses DTP messages sent by the port.
It removes 802.1Q tags from all transmitted frames.
It requires both ends to use the same access VLAN.
It changes the native VLAN to VLAN 1.
It leaves the static trunk able to carry tagged VLAN traffic.
explanation: The command stops the port from sending DTP messages. It does not change 802.1Q tagging, so the static trunk keeps carrying tagged VLANs.

whyWrong.1: Disabling DTP does not disable 802.1Q tagging.
whyWrong.2: The command has no access VLAN requirement.
whyWrong.3: The native VLAN stays whatever the trunk is configured with.

prompt: An engineer removes VLAN 1 from a Catalyst trunk's allowed list. What is the result?
options: All Cisco discovery and negotiation messages stop on the link.
The trunk's native VLAN automatically becomes the lowest allowed VLAN.
VLAN 1 user forwarding is restricted, but some link-control protocols can still operate.
The trunk becomes an access port in its configured native VLAN.
explanation: The allowed list controls which VLANs the trunk forwards. Link-control protocols such as CDP, PAgP and DTP still run in VLAN 1 even when VLAN 1 is removed.

whyWrong.0: Control protocols such as CDP, PAgP and DTP keep running.
whyWrong.1: The native VLAN is a separate setting and does not change.
whyWrong.3: Editing the allowed list does not change the port mode.

exhibit.title: Representative excerpt — SW1# show interfaces trunk
exhibit.text:
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1       on           802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       10,20,30,99

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/1       10,20,99

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/1       10,20,99

prompt: VLAN 30 cannot cross SW1's trunk. What does the exhibit show?
options: VLAN 30 is allowed but is not active locally.
VLAN 30 is missing from the configured allowed list.
VLAN 30 is active but held out of forwarding by STP.
VLAN 30 is the trunk's untagged native VLAN.
explanation: VLAN 30 is in the allowed list but missing from the active list. A VLAN that is allowed but not active is missing or inactive in the local VLAN database.

whyWrong.1: VLAN 30 is in the allowed list.
whyWrong.2: The exhibit shows no STP state, and VLAN 30 is already missing from the active list.

prompt: The peer is in dynamic auto with DTP enabled. Which two local modes can form a trunk? (Choose two.)
options: Static access
Dynamic auto
Static trunk with DTP enabled
Dynamic desirable
Static access with VLAN 99
explanation: Dynamic desirable sends trunk requests that an auto peer accepts. A static trunk with DTP enabled also advertises trunking, so an auto peer joins it.

whyWrong.1: Auto with auto is passive on both sides.
whyWrong.4: The access VLAN value does not change the port mode.

exhibit.title: Configuration excerpts from the two trunk ports
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1:
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99,999

SW2 Gi0/1:
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 999
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99,999

prompt: The design calls for native VLAN 99 at both ends. Which single change fixes the mismatch?
options: On SW1, change its allowed list to VLAN 999 only.
On SW2, add VLAN 99 as an access VLAN.
On SW1, change its switchport mode to dynamic auto.
On SW2, set switchport trunk native vlan 99.
explanation: The native VLAN is set per trunk port. Setting SW2's native VLAN to 99 makes both ends match.

whyWrong.0: The allowed list does not set the native VLAN.
whyWrong.1: An access VLAN does not set the trunk's native VLAN.
whyWrong.2: The port mode does not set the native VLAN.

prompt: Gi0/1 currently allows VLANs 10,20,99. Which command adds VLAN 30 while preserving that list?
options: switchport access vlan 30
switchport trunk allowed vlan 30
switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
switchport trunk native vlan 30
explanation: The add keyword extends the existing allowed list. A bare list replaces the whole list and can cut off other VLANs.

whyWrong.0: This assigns an access VLAN and does not touch the trunk's allowed list.
whyWrong.1: This replaces the list with VLAN 30 only.
whyWrong.3: This changes the native VLAN, not the allowed list.

exhibit.title: Representative older-platform configuration rejection
exhibit.text:
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Command rejected: An interface whose trunk encapsulation is "Auto" can not be configured to "trunk" mode.

prompt: This interface supports a choice of encapsulation and rejected static trunk mode. Which command fixes the rejection?
options: switchport trunk native vlan 1
switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
switchport nonegotiate
switchport access vlan 10
explanation: Interfaces that support more than one encapsulation need switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q before switchport mode trunk. A 2960 supports only 802.1Q and does not need it.

whyWrong.0: The native VLAN does not select the encapsulation.
whyWrong.2: nonegotiate stops DTP and does not select the encapsulation.
whyWrong.3: An access VLAN does not resolve the encapsulation error.

prompt: A trunk has native VLAN 99. It receives an untagged data frame. Which VLAN does the switch put it in?
options: Into VLAN 1 because the frame has no explicit VID.
Into the access VLAN configured on that same trunk port.
Into every VLAN in the trunk's allowed list.
Into VLAN 99 according to the receiving trunk's native setting.
explanation: An untagged frame on a trunk belongs to the receiving port's native VLAN. Here that is VLAN 99.

whyWrong.0: VLAN 1 is only the default native VLAN, and this port is set to 99.
whyWrong.1: A trunk port uses its native VLAN, not an access VLAN, for untagged frames.
whyWrong.2: A frame belongs to exactly one VLAN.

exhibit.title: Configured trunk settings
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1: mode trunk; native 99; allowed 10,99
SW2 Gi0/1: mode trunk; native 99; allowed 10,20,99

prompt: VLANs 10 and 20 are active on both switches and the PC ports are correct. VLAN 10 crosses the link and VLAN 20 does not. What is the cause?
options: SW1 classifies all tagged VLAN 20 data into native VLAN 99.
SW1's trunk omits VLAN 20 from its allowed list.
The static trunks require DTP before they can carry VLAN 20.
SW2 has no active local VLAN 20 to receive the tagged traffic.
explanation: VLAN 10 works and VLAN 20 does not, so the trunk is up and one allowed list leaves out VLAN 20. Add VLAN 20 to SW1's list with add and retest.

whyWrong.0: The native VLAN rule applies only to untagged frames, not to tagged VLAN 20 traffic.
whyWrong.2: Static trunks carry VLANs without DTP.
whyWrong.3: The question states that VLAN 20 is active on both switches.

prompt: An untagged Ethernet frame is 1,518 bytes, destination MAC through FCS. How long is it with one 802.1Q tag added?
options: 1,522 bytes
1,514 bytes
1,526 bytes
1,500 bytes
explanation: An 802.1Q tag adds 4 bytes, so 1,518 becomes 1,522. The count excludes preamble and start delimiter.

whyWrong.1: The tag adds 4 bytes, so the frame gets longer.
whyWrong.2: That adds 8 bytes, which is two tags.
whyWrong.3: 1,500 bytes is the usual maximum payload, not the frame length.

prompt: A PC must use untagged VLAN 10 only and must not negotiate a trunk. Which configuration fits?
options: switchport mode dynamic desirable; switchport access vlan 10
switchport mode access; switchport access vlan 10
switchport mode trunk; switchport trunk native vlan 10
switchport mode dynamic auto; switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
explanation: switchport mode access makes the port a static access port, and switchport access vlan 10 puts it in VLAN 10. Static access also disables DTP negotiation.

whyWrong.0: Desirable actively tries to form a trunk.
whyWrong.2: A trunk stays a trunk whatever its native VLAN.
whyWrong.3: Dynamic auto can still become a trunk if the peer asks.

exhibit.title: AP requirements and switch port configuration
exhibit.text:
AP: management untagged in VLAN 100; staff tagged 110; guests tagged 120.
Switch interface:
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 100,110,120
 switchport nonegotiate

prompt: The AP needs untagged management VLAN 100 and tagged client VLANs 110 and 120. Which switch change fixes the configuration shown?
options: Set the port to access VLAN 100.
Remove VLAN 100 from the allowed list.
Set the native VLAN to 110.
Set the native VLAN to 100.
explanation: Untagged frames from the AP are classified into the native VLAN. Setting the native VLAN to 100 puts management in VLAN 100 while 110 and 120 stay tagged.

whyWrong.0: An access port cannot carry tagged VLANs 110 and 120.
whyWrong.1: Removing VLAN 100 from the allowed list would block management traffic.
whyWrong.2: Native VLAN 110 would put untagged management traffic into a client VLAN.

exhibit.title: Virtual-host uplink requirements supplied by its administrator
exhibit.text:
Management interface: VLAN 100 tagged
VM group A: VLAN 110 tagged
VM group B: VLAN 120 tagged
No service uses untagged traffic; unused native VLAN 999 agreed.

prompt: A virtual host needs VLANs 100, 110 and 120 all tagged on its uplink. Which switch profile keeps all three tagged?
options: Allow 100,110,120 and use an agreed unused native VLAN 999.
Allow 100,110,120 and make management VLAN 100 native.
Use access VLAN 110 because the virtual switch handles all VLANs.
Allow only VLAN 999 and make management VLAN 100 native.
explanation: Default native treatment removes the tag from native VLAN frames. Using an unused native VLAN such as 999 keeps VLANs 100, 110 and 120 tagged.

whyWrong.1: Native VLAN 100 would send management frames untagged.
whyWrong.2: One access VLAN cannot carry three tagged VLANs.
whyWrong.3: VLANs 100, 110 and 120 are missing from that allowed list.

prompt: A firewall has logical interfaces for tagged VLANs 10 and 20 and does not use DTP. What goes on the switch port?
options: Dynamic auto with access VLAN 10.
A routed switch port with no switchport and no IP address.
A static trunk permitting VLANs 10 and 20, with matching native treatment.
An access port in VLAN 20 with an additional allowed list.
explanation: Tagged VLANs from a device need a static trunk that allows those VLANs. The firewall does not use DTP, so the switch must be set to trunk statically.

whyWrong.0: Auto needs a peer that negotiates, and the firewall does not.
whyWrong.1: A routed port is not a Layer 2 trunk.
whyWrong.3: An allowed list does not turn an access port into a trunk.

exhibit.title: Representative local trunk excerpt
exhibit.text:
Gi0/1: trunking, native VLAN 99
Vlans allowed: 10,20,99
Vlans allowed and active: 10,20,99
Vlans forwarding and not pruned: 10,99

prompt: VLAN 20 is missing from only the last list. What does that show?
options: VLAN 20 is not currently eligible to forward on this port.
VLAN 20 was removed from the configured allowed list.
VLAN 20 is absent from the local VLAN database.
VLAN 20 is being forwarded without an 802.1Q tag.
explanation: The last list shows VLANs that are allowed, active and forwarding. Missing from it only means VLAN 20 is not forwarding on this port, so check spanning-tree or pruning next.

whyWrong.1: VLAN 20 is in the configured allowed list.
whyWrong.2: VLAN 20 is in the allowed-and-active list.
whyWrong.3: The native VLAN is 99, so VLAN 20 is not untagged.

exhibit.title: Supplied relevant local checks
exhibit.text:
show interfaces trunk: Gi0/2 absent
Gi0/2 switchport: administrative mode trunk
Gi0/2 interface state: administratively down
VLANs 10,20,99: active; allowed list 10,20,99

prompt: The link is approved, the peer is configured to match and the cable is connected. What is the next action?
options: Recreate VLANs 10 and 20 because native VLAN 99 prevents trunking.
Replace the allowed list with all VLANs to make the port operational.
Assign an IP address directly to the Layer 2 trunk interface.
Enable Gi0/2 with no shutdown, then verify its actual operational state.
explanation: A port that is administratively shut down will not come up. Enter no shutdown on Gi0/2, then check the operational state.

whyWrong.0: An unused native VLAN does not stop a static trunk.
whyWrong.1: Allowing more VLANs does not remove a shutdown.
whyWrong.2: A Layer 2 trunk takes no IP address.

prompt: SW1 sends a frame from native VLAN 99 and SW2's native VLAN is 999. Both VLANs are allowed and active. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)
options: SW1 sends this native-VLAN frame without an 802.1Q tag.
SW1 changes the frame's source MAC to identify VLAN 99.
SW2 uses VLAN 99 because the sender's original membership is retained invisibly.
SW2 classifies the received untagged frame into VLAN 999.
SW2 puts the frame into both native VLANs simultaneously.
explanation: A trunk sends native VLAN frames untagged. The receiver puts untagged frames into its own native VLAN, here 999.

whyWrong.1: Tagging never rewrites the source MAC.
whyWrong.2: An untagged frame carries no VLAN ID, so VLAN 99 is lost.
whyWrong.4: A frame goes into one VLAN, the receiver's native VLAN.

prompt: SW1 is a static trunk with nonegotiate and SW2 is dynamic auto, so SW2 stays an access port. Which change builds the trunk without DTP?
options: Configure SW2 as a static trunk with the matching native/allowed settings.
Change SW1's native VLAN to SW2's access VLAN without changing modes.
Keep both modes and clear the dynamic MAC tables.
Keep both modes and create management SVIs on the switches.
explanation: SW1 sends no DTP, so a passive auto port never trunks. Configure SW2 as a static trunk with the matching native and allowed VLANs.

whyWrong.1: Matching an access VLAN does not make SW2 a trunk.
whyWrong.2: Clearing the MAC table does not change the port mode.
whyWrong.3: SVIs do not change the port mode.

exhibit.title: Supplied operational trunk summaries; native 99 at both ends
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1: trunking
 allowed: 10,20,30,40,99
 allowed and active: 10,20,30,99
 forwarding and not pruned: 10,20,99
SW2 Gi0/1: trunking
 allowed: 10,20,30,40,99
 allowed and active: 10,20,30,40,99
 forwarding and not pruned: 20,30,40,99

prompt: Which VLAN can cross this link in both directions?
options: VLANs 10 and 20
VLAN 20
VLANs 20 and 30
explanation: A VLAN crosses only if it is forwarding on both ends. Only VLAN 20 is in the forwarding list at both ends.

whyWrong.0: VLAN 10 is not forwarding on SW2.
whyWrong.2: VLAN 30 is not forwarding on SW1.
whyWrong.3: Several of those VLANs are not active or forwarding at one end.

exhibit.title: Supplied rollout verification
exhibit.text:
New PCs: 192.168.30.11/24 on SW1 Fa0/3; 192.168.30.12/24 on SW2 Fa0/3
SW1 Fa0/3: access VLAN 10
SW2 Fa0/3: access VLAN 30
VLANs 10,20,30,99 active on both switches
Both uplinks: static trunk, native 99
SW1 uplink allowed: 10,20,30,99
SW2 uplink allowed: 10,20,99
Existing VLAN 10 and 20 client pairs work

prompt: The VLAN 30 pair must communicate and VLANs 10 and 20 must keep working. Which two corrections are required? (Choose two.)
options: Set SW1 Fa0/3 to access VLAN 30.
Replace SW1's uplink allowed list with VLAN 30 only.
Set both uplink native VLANs to 30.
Add VLAN 30 to SW2's existing uplink allowed list.
Move SW2 Fa0/3 to access VLAN 10.
explanation: SW1's new endpoint is in the wrong access VLAN, and SW2's trunk does not allow VLAN 30. Use add on the trunk so VLANs 10 and 20 stay allowed.

whyWrong.1: Replacing the list with VLAN 30 breaks VLANs 10 and 20.
whyWrong.2: The native VLAN does not fix the access port or the allowed list.
whyWrong.4: The new pair belongs in VLAN 30, not VLAN 10.

prompt: What is the default mode of a Catalyst 2960 switch port?
options: Static access
Dynamic auto
Dynamic desirable
Static trunk
explanation: A 2960 port defaults to dynamic auto. It becomes a trunk only if the other end asks.

whyWrong.0: Access is a configured mode, not the default.
whyWrong.2: Desirable actively asks for a trunk and is not the default.
whyWrong.3: A static trunk must be configured.

prompt: What is the default native VLAN on a Cisco switch trunk?
options: VLAN 0
VLAN 1
VLAN 99
VLAN 1002
explanation: The native VLAN is VLAN 1 by default. Its frames cross the trunk untagged.

whyWrong.0: VLAN 0 is reserved and is not a usable VLAN.
whyWrong.2: VLAN 99 is a common choice for a custom native VLAN, not the default.
whyWrong.3: VLAN 1002 is a reserved legacy VLAN.

prompt: Which two VLAN IDs are reserved and not usable?
explanation: Usable VLAN IDs are 1–4094. VLAN IDs 0 and 4095 are reserved.

whyWrong.0: VLAN 1 is usable, and 1005 is a legacy range VLAN.
whyWrong.2: VLAN 1 and VLAN 4094 are both usable.

prompt: What does 802.1Q tagging do?
options: It routes traffic between VLANs.
It identifies the VLAN a frame belongs to.
It encrypts frames on the trunk.
It chooses the spanning-tree root.
explanation: A tag carries the frame's VLAN ID across a shared link. Routing between VLANs needs a Layer 3 device.

whyWrong.0: Tagging preserves VLANs and does not route between them.
whyWrong.2: 802.1Q does not encrypt anything.
whyWrong.3: The root is chosen by bridge ID, not by tags.
